questions.problem: A bolt manufacturer determines that $1.5%$ of the bolts produced are defective. A quality control inspection will check $200$ randomly selected bolts. What is the mean number of defective bolts in the sample?
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of defective bolts in the sample.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=200$ bolts

- the probability of selecting a defective bolt is $p=1.5%=0.015$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(200,0.015).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the mean is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the mean number of defective bolts is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =(200)(0.015) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(80,\frac{1}{6}).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the standard deviation is given by

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the  number of times we get a number divisible by $5$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{np(1-p)} \\  & =\sqrt{80\cdot \frac{1}{6}\cdot (1-\frac{1}{6})} \\  & =\sqrt{80\cdot \frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{5}{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{100}{9}} \\  & =\frac{10}{3}.\end{aligned}

                    Finding the Standard Deviation of a Binomial Random Variable
canonical_examples.problem: A fair five-sided die is rolled $8$ times. What is the standard deviation of the number of times we get an even number? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times we get an even number.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=8$ rolls of the die

- the probability of getting an even number (i.e., a $2,$ or $4$) on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\dfrac{2}{5} .
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B\left(8,\dfrac25\right).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the standard deviation is given by

$$
\textrm{SD}[X] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the number of times we get an even number is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{np(1-p)} \\  & =\sqrt{8\cdot \frac{2}{5}\cdot (1-\frac{2}{5})} \\  & =\sqrt{1.92} \\  & =1.386\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Remember that if $X$ is a binomial random variable in which there are $n$ experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment, then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}.
$$

It can be shown that the expected value, variance, and standard deviation of a binomial random variable $X$ can be computed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\ \text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{np(1-p)}\end{aligned}
$$
